settings.heading: What Is Puff Print?
settings.answer: Puff print is a raised, 3D printing effect made by mixing a heat-reactive additive into screen-printing ink — when the print cures, the ink expands into a soft, foam-like texture you can feel. It works best on cotton and cotton-blend blanks, and the look can also be made with puff HTV or puff DTF transfers.

settings.text: Puff print is a raised, 3D effect: a heat-reactive additive is mixed into the ink, and it expands into a soft foam when the print is cured under high heat.
Three ways to get it — puff additive in screen-print ink (best for runs), puff HTV (cut-and-press, great for small custom jobs), and puff DTF transfers (raised plus full color).
It works best on cotton and cotton blends, especially midweight and heavyweight — and on bold solid shapes or block text, not fine lines or small detail.
Puff ink feels soft and flexible and moves with the fabric, giving custom apparel a tactile, premium look that reads more expensive.
Cared for right it lasts 50+ washes: turn the garment inside out, wash cold, skip bleach, and air-dry or tumble low — hot water weakens the bond and can crack it.
Opaque puff ink covers darks with no separate underbase, and it can print on polyester too — though cotton gives the cleanest rise.

settings.question: What is puff print?
settings.answer: Puff print is a printing technique that creates a raised, three-dimensional design that stands up off the fabric. It's a variation of screen printing: a special heat-reactive additive is mixed into the ink, and when the print passes through a high-heat dryer the additive expands, puffing the ink into a soft, foam-like texture you can feel. The same raised look can also be made with puff heat-transfer vinyl or puff DTF transfers.

settings.question: How does the puff effect actually work?
settings.answer: The puff additive is made of tiny microspheres that expand when they reach a specific temperature. It's blended into plastisol screen-printing ink, printed onto the garment through a stencil, then cured under heat. As the ink heats, the microspheres swell and lift the print off the surface, creating the raised 3D effect. The amount of rise depends on the additive ratio and the cure temperature.

settings.question: Is puff print the same as embroidery?
settings.answer: No. Both add dimension, but puff print is raised ink and embroidery is stitched thread. Puff is faster and cheaper for bold solid graphics and gives a soft, rubbery feel; embroidery is stitched into the fabric for a premium, durable, textured logo that suits polos, caps, and fleece. Puff reads as streetwear and graphic apparel; embroidery reads as uniform and corporate.

settings.question: What fabric is best for puff print?
settings.answer: Cotton and cotton-blend garments give the best results, especially midweight and heavyweight fabrics where the surface is stable enough for the ink to rise cleanly. Puff can be printed on polyester and blends too, but poly needs a lower cure temperature and the rise is slightly less pronounced. Smooth-faced, solid-color blanks puff the cleanest.

settings.question: Does puff print crack or peel over time?
settings.answer: Quality puff print is durable and routinely lasts 50 or more washes without cracking when it's cared for. The thing that damages it is heat: hot water and high-heat drying weaken the bond and can cause cracking or peeling. To make it last, turn the garment inside out, wash in cold water, skip the bleach and harsh detergent, and air-dry or tumble on low. Avoid ironing directly over the print.

settings.question: Puff additive, puff HTV, or puff DTF — which should I use?
settings.answer: Puff additive (screen printing) is most cost-effective for medium-to-large runs of a bold, few-color design. Puff HTV is cut-and-press vinyl that's ideal for small custom runs, names, and numbers with no screens to set up. Puff DTF transfers let you combine raised puff elements with full-color, photographic detail — the most versatile option for one-offs and complex art. Choose by run size and how much detail and color the design needs.
